topic: How Does the Internet Travel Across the Ocean Floor?
angle: Nearly 99% of all global data runs not through the 'cloud' or satellites, but through fragile glass strands thinner than a pencil resting on the bottom of the ocean.
why: Explainer videos on subsea infrastructure and hidden technology consistently cross tens of millions of views because audiences assume the modern internet is entirely wireless. The sheer absurdity of modern civilization depending on physical cables lying unprotected in deep-sea mud next to ship anchors and sharks makes the mechanism instantly compelling.
keywords: how do undersea cables get power
what happens if undersea cable breaks
facts: Undersea fiber-optic cables transmit approximately 95% to 99% of all transoceanic internet traffic, while satellites carry only a tiny fraction of global data.
There are over 550 active and planned commercial undersea fiber cables worldwide, spanning roughly 1.4 million kilometers of the Earth's seabed.
The data is transmitted through strands of ultrapure silica glass, each core measuring roughly 9 to 10 microns in diameter—about one-tenth the width of a human hair.
Information travels through the glass strands as pulses of laser light at roughly 200,000 kilometers per second, using continuous total internal reflection.
In the deepest parts of the ocean down to 8,000 meters, cables are only about 17 to 20 millimeters thick—roughly the diameter of a standard garden hose.
In deep water, human interference is virtually nonexistent, so the cable only needs a steel wire strength member, a copper power conductor, and water-blocking polyethylene insulation.

In shallow water near coastlines (depths under 1,500 meters), the cable is reinforced with multiple spiral layers of galvanized steel wire and tar-coated nylon yarn, expanding to 50 millimeters thick.
Commercial fishing trawlers and dragging ship anchors cause approximately two-thirds of all underwater cable cuts worldwide.
To protect cables near shores, specialized ships pull a 30-ton underwater plow that carves a trench 1 to 3 meters into the seabed, laying the cable inside before ocean sediment buries it.
Laser light naturally loses strength over long distances inside glass due to light scattering and microscopic material absorption.
To keep signals intact across ocean basins, optical amplifiers called repeaters are spliced into the cable every 50 to 80 kilometers.
Repeaters use erbium-doped fiber amplifiers to boost the optical signal directly using laser energy, without ever converting light back into electronic data.
To power hundreds of repeaters along a 6,000-kilometer ocean crossing, a central copper sheath carries up to 10,000 to 18,000 volts of direct current (DC).

The electric circuit is completed by the ocean itself: power stations on opposite coastlines inject power into the copper conductor, and the return path flows naturally through seawater grounding beds.
Specialized cable-laying ships, often over 140 meters long, carry thousands of kilometers of cable coiled inside massive climate-controlled cylindrical tanks below deck.
These ships utilize GPS-linked dynamic positioning thrusters to lay cable at a steady crawl of 1 to 2 knots, adjusting spool tension precisely to prevent the line from snapping or bunching.
When a deep-sea cable breaks, repair ships deploy underwater Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) or grappling hooks to lift the severed ends to the surface.

Onboard the repair ship, engineers must splice each microscopic glass fiber individually by hand inside an airtight cleanroom before sealing the joint in a waterproof housing and lowering it back down.
Modern high-capacity transatlantic cables can carry over 250 to 350 terabits of data per second on a single line, enough to stream millions of ultra-HD video feeds at the exact same moment.
An opinion piece in the Brantford Expositor argues that the majority of data is transmitted via the ocean rather than through the sky.
A publication by War on the Rocks addresses the question of who handles internet repairs during periods of armed conflict.

The Coastal Connections Journalism Fellowship in Sri Lanka is planned to be fully funded.
